e-21649.problem: Given that $\displaystyle J(t)=\int_{0}^{1} (\cos t+2x)^2\, \textrm{d}x,$ calculate $J'(t)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$ by differentiating under the integral sign.
e-21649.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R = [a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t) = \int_{a}^b f(x,t)\,\textrm{d} x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
F'(t) = \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t}\int_{a}^b f(x,t)\,\textrm{d} x
=
\int_{a}^b \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,\textrm{d} x.
$$

This is known as differentiating under the integral sign.

We wish to compute $J'(t),$ where

$$
J(t)=\int_{0}^{1} (\cos t+2x)^2\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Differentiating under the integral sign, we get

$$
J'(t) = \int_{0}^{1} \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\Bigl[(\cos t+2x)^2\Bigr]\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Next, let's compute the partial derivative with respect to $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂t}[(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2x)^{2}] & =2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2x)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2x) \\  & =2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2x)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this back into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}^{′}(t) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{\int }_{0}^{1}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's evaluate the remaining integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2x)\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot x{|}_{0}^{1}+{x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
J'(t) =-2\sin t\,(\cos t+1).
$$
